title: Acetabular osteophyte-like ossification in DDH: association with labral morphology and age

paragraphs.en: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is one of the most common hip disorders in children, with a reported incidence ranging from 1.3 to 28.5 per 1,000 children [1,2]. The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous structure at the acetabular rim [3], which is essential for maintaining hip joint stability and biomechanical function [4]. In patients with DDH, acetabular dysplasia results in insufficient coverage of the femoral head. Consequently, the labrum is subjected to abnormal stress, leading to complex adaptive or degenerative changes [5]. Miyake et al. [5,6] classified the morphology of the acetabular labrum in DDH into three types: everted, inverted, and partly inverted. In the everted type, the labrum is positioned lateral to the femoral head. In contrast, in the inverted and partly inverted types, it lies entirely or partly medial to the femoral head. A critical distinction between the pediatric and adult acetabular labrum is its anatomical connection. In children, the labrum integrates with the acetabular epiphyseal cartilage through a fibrocartilaginous transition zone, forming the labrum-acetabular cartilage complex (LACC) [7,8]. Changes in labrum shape may affect the normal development of acetabular cartilage [9].

During the development of the acetabulum in children, ossification primarily occurs through endochondral ossification [10]. Previous studies have shown that ossification of the acetabulum is impaired in patients with DDH, leading to a shallower and more oblique acetabulum on the affected side [11]. Conventional radiographic indices of impaired ossification include the acetabular index [12], center edge angle [13], and the acetabular depth width ratio [14]. However, abnormal ossification in DDH is not limited to under-development. The growth and development of the bony acetabulum in children is governed by the epiphyseal cartilage [15]. Osteogenesis of the epiphyseal cartilage drives expansion of the acetabular cavity, which utilizes the spherical shape of the femoral head as a growth template [11]. We observed that as LACC deformity progresses, acetabular cartilage loses support from the spherical femoral head template, preventing outward extension. Instead, the acetabular cartilage is compressed by the femoral head, bending inward and downward, and undergo premature osteophyte-like abnormal ossification. Previous animal experiments suggested that this might be related to cartilage degeneration associated with LACC inversion [16,17]. However, there is currently no clinical study on the correlation between LACC morphology and AOO. AOO alters the smooth and curved morphology of the acetabulum, compromising its congruence with the femoral head (Figure 1), with potential implications for acetabular remodeling and long-term prognosis. From a treatment perspective, such morphological alterations might affect decisions regarding closed versus open reduction by creating a bony obstacle to concentric reduction, and may also influence labral management strategies – for example, whether isolated labral incision suffices or concurrent management of the ossific protrusion is required. However, large-scale longitudinal studies are lacking, and its long-term clinical impact remains unconfirmed. Previous evidence linking LACC morphology to such ossification is limited to animal experiments [16,17], clinical data in humans are absent. In this study, we aim to investigate the imaging correlates of AOO as a foundational step toward defining its clinical relevance in preoperative planning.

This study aims to find the correlation between LACC morphology and AOO and to assess the influence of age on the abnormal ossification by reviewing preoperative hip MRI and CT images of patients with DDH. Crucially, we sought to determine whether the role of LACC morphology is age-dependent – that is, whether its predictive value for AOO emerges specifically in older children, independent of DDH severity.

We retrospectively collected preoperative anteroposterior pelvic radiographs, hip MRI and CT images of patients diagnosed with DDH at our hospital between January 2015 and December 2022. The inclusion criteria were 1) patients diagnosed with DDH based on plain radiographs or CT and 2) no prior treatment before these imaging examinations. The exclusion criteria were 1) absence of coronal MRI images or poor image quality precluding assessment of LACC morphology; 2) CT reconstruction slice thickness >1 mm precluding three-dimensional analysis; 3) interval between CT and MRI examinations exceeding one month and 4) absence of standard preoperative anteroposterior pelvic radiographs or poor radiographic quality precluding radiographic assessment. All radiographic, MRI, and CT examinations were obtained as part of the preoperative evaluation, no treatment was performed during the interval between these imaging examinations. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 180 patients (199 affected hips) were ultimately included (Figure 2). This study was approved by our hospital’s ethics committee (No. 2025-389) which covers retrospective analysis of imaging data from the full study period of January 2015 to December 2022. The requirement for informed consent was waived by the ethics committee due to the retrospective nature of the study, which involved the analysis of anonymized imaging data. All procedures performed in studies involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments. Data analysis for this study began on October 1, 2025.

Preoperative standard anteroposterior pelvic radiographs were reviewed to evaluate acetabular development and radiographic DDH severity. AI was measured on the affected side as the angle between Hilgenreiner’s line and the acetabular roof line and was recorded in degrees [18]. Radiographic DDH severity was assessed using the Tönnis classification [19]. In the logistic regression analyses, AI was entered as a continuous variable, whereas Tönnis classification was dichotomized into grades I–II and grades III–IV to reduce model instability caused by small subgroup sizes and to facilitate multivariable adjustment. Disagreements in radiographic assessment were resolved by consensus review.

T2-weighted fat-suppressed coronal MRI images of hips were retrieved from our hospital’s Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). The images were reviewed independently by two pediatric radiologists, each with over ten years of experience. According to the Miyake classification (Figure 3), the shape of LACC on the affected side was classified. Hips were subsequently divided into two groups based on LACC morphology: the everted group and the inverted group (the latter including completely inverted and partly inverted subtypes). Because both partly inverted and completely inverted LACC represent varying degrees of medial displacement of the LACC toward the femoral head and may interfere with concentric hip reduction, these two subtypes were combined into the inverted LACC group for the main analysis. Patients were also divided into two age subgroups: ≤2 years and >2 years.

Axial thin-slice CT images of bilateral hips were retrieved from our hospital’s PACS and loaded onto the GE workstation for multi-planar reconstruction (MPR). All CT examinations were performed using a tube voltage of 100–120 kVp, with tube current adjusted according to our institution’s pediatric dose optimization protocols (range approximately 40–250 mAs, varying by patient age, body size, and scanner type). The pitch ranged from 0.8 to 1.4, the reconstruction matrix was 512 × 512 pixels, and axial images were reconstructed at 1.0 mm slice thickness for MPR. Patients with CT reconstruction slice thickness >1.0 mm were excluded from the study to ensure adequate spatial resolution for detecting subtle ossifications. AOO was defined as follows: on MPR-generated coronal images of the acetabulum, consecutive slices of acetabula were selected. Using the triradiate cartilage as the reference starting point, a circumference was drawn along the contour of the bony acetabulum. Any bony protrusion extending inward beyond the circumference traced along the osseous acetabular margin was considered AOO (Figure 4). On sagittal reconstructions, the acetabulum was divided into anterior and posterior regions to assess the presence and location of the ossification, and its distribution ratio was calculated.

MRI assessment of LACC morphology and CT evaluation of AOO were performed independently by two pediatric radiologists (A and B). To assess intra-observer variability, one radiologist conducted two blinded evaluations at an interval of two months. Inter-observer variability was determined through independent assessments by both radiologists.

SPSS (version 27.0, IBM, Chicago, IL, USA) was used for statistical analyses. Continuous variables with a normal distribution were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) and compared using the independent-samples t test. Continuous variables with a skewed distribution were presented as the median and interquartile range [M (Q1, Q3)] and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were reported as numbers and percentages [n (%)] and compared using Pearson’s chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. To enhance the presentation of incidence data, 95% confidence intervals for the incidence rates were calculated using the Clopper-Pearson exact method for binomial proportions. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was constructed to assess the predictive value of age for the abnormal ossification in each morphologic group.

To adjust for potential confounding by DDH severity, multivariable logistic regression was performed with AOO as the dependent variable, and LACC morphology, age (months), acetabular index, and Tönnis grade (binary: I–II vs. III–IV) as independent variables. Subgroup analyses were also performed in patients >2 years of age. Variance inflation factor (VIF) was calculated to assess multicollinearity among covariates. To formally evaluate whether the effect of LACC morphology on AOO varies with age, we tested the interaction term between LACC group (inverted vs. everted) and age (continuous) in the logistic regression model. For each multivariable logistic regression model, the number of AOO events and the events per predictor variable (EPV), calculated as the number of AOO-positive hips divided by the number of predictor parameters included in the corresponding model, were reported. A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Intra- and inter-observer variability was quantified using Cohen’s kappa (k), with the following interpretations: poor (k ≤ 0.20), fair (0.20 < k ≤ 0.40), moderate (0.40 < k ≤ 0.60), good (0.60 < k ≤ 0.80), and excellent (k > 0.80). All estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

This study included a total of 180 patients (199 affected hips) with DDH. Among the patients, 150 were female and 30 were male; 161 patients had unilateral DDH and 19 had bilateral involvement. Baseline characteristics of affected hips according to LACC morphology are presented in Table 1. According to the original three-subtype LACC classification, 53 hips were classified as everted, 43 as partly inverted, and 103 as completely inverted (Supplementary Table S1). For the primary analysis, the partly inverted and completely inverted subtypes were combined into the inverted LACC group, resulting in 146 hips in the inverted group and 53 hips in the everted group. As shown in Table 1, the inverted LACC group had a significantly higher acetabular index and a greater proportion of Tönnis grade III–IV compared with the everted group.

AOO was identified in 44/146 (30.1%) inverted hips and 10/53 (18.9%) everted hips. The incidence across different LACC groups and age strata is presented in Table 2. As shown in Table 2, the incidence of AOO was significantly higher in the inverted LACC group than in the everted group among children >2 years (p = 0.031, chi-square test), whereas no significant difference was observed in the ≤2-year subgroup (p = 0.515, Fisher’s exact test).

The distribution of ossification sites by LACC morphology is presented in Table 3. In the inverted group, isolated posterior acetabular ossification was predominant, accounting for 70.4% of AOO-positive hips, followed by anterior ossification (20.5%) and combined anterior–posterior involvement (9.1%). In the everted group, the distribution was relatively balanced, with anterior, posterior, and combined lesions accounting for 50.0%, 40.0%, and 10.0%, respectively. On contemporaneous MRI, the AOO lesions were surrounded by relatively thick acetabular cartilage (Figure 5).

Multivariable logistic regression adjusting for LACC morphology, age, AI, and Tönnis grade demonstrated that age remained the most robust independent correlate of AOO across the entire cohort (OR = 1.022, 95% CI: 1.013–1.032, p < 0.001), whereas LACC morphology (p = 0.105), AI (p = 0.092), and Tönnis grade (p = 0.801) were not significant in the full model (Table 4). In a sensitivity analysis excluding AI (Supplementary Table S2), LACC morphology became significantly associated with AOO (OR = 3.792, 95% CI: 1.346–10.683, p = 0.012), while age (OR = 1.022, 95% CI: 1.013–1.032, p < 0.001) remained significant and Tönnis grade did not. In children aged >2 years, inverted LACC was independently associated with AOO (OR = 7.66, 95% CI: 1.703–34.465, p = 0.008), while age (p = 0.148) and AI (p = 0.505) were not statistically significant. Tönnis grade showed an inverse association with AOO in this subgroup (OR = 0.237, 95% CI: 0.069–0.814, p = 0.022); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the limited subgroup sample size and potential residual confounding (Table 5). VIF values for all covariates were <5, indicating no significant multicollinearity. The interaction between LACC morphology and age was statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.042) in the Supplementary Table S3, confirming that the association between labral inversion and AOO is age-dependent. The numbers of hips analyzed, AOO events, predictor parameters, and corresponding EPVs for each multivariable model are summarized in Supplementary Table S4.

ROC curve analysis demonstrated that age predicted AOO in both LACC groups, with a higher AUC in the inverted group (80.0%, 95% CI: 0.72–0.88) compared with the everted group (73.5%, 95% CI: 0.57–0.89). The optimal age cutoff was 22.5 months for the inverted group (sensitivity: 0.795, specificity: 0.725) and 30.5 months for the everted group (sensitivity: 0.800, specificity: 0.674) (Figure 6).

All radiographic assessments demonstrated excellent reliability. For intra-observer agreement of the LACC classification, the Cohen’s kappa was 0.90 (95% CI: 0.83–0.97) for A and 0.94 (95% CI: 0.88–0.99) for B. For inter-observer agreement, the kappa value was 0.87 (95% CI: 0.79–0.95). For intra-observer agreement of the presence of AOO on CT, the intra-observer kappa was 0.91 (95% CI: 0.85–0.98) for A and 0.94 (95% CI: 0.88–0.99) for B, and the inter-observer kappa was 0.86 (95% CI: 0.78–0.94). For the location of AOO on CT (anterior, posterior, or both), the intra-observer kappa was 0.96 (95% CI: 0.89–0.99) for both A and B, and the inter-observer kappa was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.83–0.99).

In this cross-sectional cohort, age emerged as the most consistent independent correlate of AOO across all ages. However, the role of LACC morphology was age-dependent: in children >2 years of age, inverted LACC was strongly and independently associated with AOO. The significant interaction between LACC morphology and age further confirmed that the predictive value of LACC morphology for AOO is not uniform across ages but emerges specifically in older children. These findings suggest that age reflects disease chronicity, while LACC morphology functions as an age-specific risk modifier that becomes particularly relevant in older children.

DDH patients frequently exhibit LACC morphological changes. The inverted labrum serves as a critical obstacle to achieving concentric reduction between the femoral head and the acetabulum [20,21], and is hypothesized to impede normal hip development and stability, thereby influencing clinical outcomes and long-term prognosis. While most existing research has focused on the obstructive role of the labrum itself during DDH reduction and its related complications, previous studies have indicated that an inverted labrum is associated with decreased joint congruency, alter hip biomechanics, accelerate cartilage wear and hyaline cartilage degeneration [16], and may contribute to the development of early osteoarthritis [22,23]. Additionally, it may be associated with the formation of osteophytes at the acetabular rim [24]. However, few studies have explored the correlation between morphological changes in the LACC and abnormal acetabular ossification. In our research, we noted that in patients with DDH whose LACC was either completely or partially inverted, AOO was observed on the corresponding side of the acetabulum. The abnormal ossification of acetabular cartilages morphologically resembled osteophyte formation and appeared in the early stage of DDH. These AOOs may disrupt the normal smooth, curved contour of the acetabulum, potentially resulting in mismatch between the femoral head and the acetabulum. This morphological alteration may theoretically influence treatment efficacy and long-term acetabular remodeling; however, these potential effects remain speculative and require longitudinal validation. We emphasize that all such mechanistic interpretations are associative and hypothesis-generating, as our cross-sectional design cannot establish temporal or causal relationships.

We acknowledge that the term ‘osteophyte-like’ is a descriptive, imaging-based designation. These ossifications were surrounded by relatively thick acetabular cartilage on contemporaneous MRI – a finding distinct from degenerative osteophytes, which typically exhibit thin or absent overlying cartilage. The term ‘osteophyte-like’ was chosen to reflect the morphological resemblance of these lesions to osteophytes on CT, rather than to imply histopathological equivalence or classical degenerative osteophytes.

Our study revealed that in children under 2 years old, both everted and inverted LACC were associated with a similarly low incidence of AOO, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p = 0.515). This suggests that in DDH patient treatment before age 2, most acetabula exhibit a smooth, arcuate morphology, consistent with earlier findings of better treatment outcomes in DDH patients under 2 years old. However, in patients older than 2 years, the incidence of the abnormal ossification was significantly higher in those with inverted LACC compared to the everted group (p = 0.031). This indicates that beyond the age of 2, pre-treatment LACC inversion is associated with a greater risk of the abnormal ossification and thus may lead to different treatment outcomes compared to patients with everted LACC. Previous studies have primarily stratified DDH management based on patient age alone [25,26] without distinguishing these two distinct LACC morphological types in comparative analyses. Our multivariable analysis demonstrated that age remained the most robust independent correlate of AOO across the entire cohort after adjusting for DDH severity parameters (OR = 1.022, p < 0.001), supporting that age’s contribution is not merely a surrogate for severity. AI showed a trend toward association (OR = 1.059, p = 0.092), while LACC morphology did not reach independent significance in the full model (OR = 2.529, p = 0.105). However, in a sensitivity analysis excluding AI, LACC morphology became significantly associated with AOO (OR = 3.792, p = 0.012). This attenuation upon inclusion of AI indicates that AI acts as a confounding factor in the relationship between LACC morphology and AOO – consistent with the observation that more severe acetabular dysplasia is associated with both labral inversion and abnormal ossification. Notably, in the >2-year subgroup, this confounding effect was no longer present: AI was not significant (p = 0.505), while inverted LACC maintained a strong independent association with AOO (OR = 7.66, p = 0.008). This suggests that, in older children, inverted LACC remained independently associated with AOO after adjustment for baseline acetabular dysplasia. The significant interaction between age and LACC morphology (p = 0.042) further supports that the predictive value of LACC morphology is age-dependent, rather than a uniform effect across all ages. This interaction aligns with our stratified analysis showing that LACC morphology independently predicts AOO exclusively in the >2-year subgroup, and provides formal statistical confirmation that age modifies the relationship between labral shape and acetabular ossification.

To assess the stability of our multivariable models, we calculated the events per predictor variable (EPV) for each analysis (Supplementary Table S4). The EPV for the primary full-cohort model was 13.5, the sensitivity model excluding AI was 18.0, and the age–LACC interaction model was 10.8, all exceeding the conventional benchmark of approximately 10. These EPV values support the relative stability of the parameter estimates in these primary and sensitivity analyses. Nevertheless, several adjusted odds-ratio estimates, particularly those for LACC morphology in the sensitivity and >2-year subgroup analyses, had wide 95% confidence intervals, indicating limited precision. This was especially evident in the >2-year subgroup (OR = 7.660, 95% CI: 1.703–34.465), likely because of the limited number of AOO events and imbalance between the LACC groups. Notably, the EPV for this >2-year subgroup model was 9.8, which falls slightly below the conventional benchmark, further supporting the cautious interpretation of this subgroup analysis. Therefore, although the findings support the direction of the association, its exact magnitude remains uncertain and should be regarded as exploratory pending validation in larger cohorts.

Furthermore, we conducted ROC curve analysis to evaluate the association between age and the occurrence of AOO in the everted LACC group. The analysis yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 73.5%, with an optimal age cutoff of 30.5 months. This result indicates a moderate association between age and AOO in this group, suggesting that acetabular morphology in patients with everted LACC may remain relatively stable over time and may not undergo substantial ossification with advancing age. In contrast, the inverted LACC group showed a distinct pattern, with ROC analysis demonstrating a higher AUC of 80.0% and an optimal cutoff at 22.5 months. This finding implies a potentially stronger age-related association with AOO in patients with inverted LACC. However, whether this reflects a more progressive time-dependent ossification process remains speculative and should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating interpretation. Therefore, for these patients, if these findings are confirmed in future studies, earlier intervention might be considered to prevent progressive dysplastic changes and preserve the normal smooth bony acetabular morphology. While these age cutoffs may serve as a reference for risk awareness – suggesting that the likelihood of AOO increases more rapidly after approximately 22.5 months in children with inverted LACC – their clinical utility remains unproven, as our cross-sectional design cannot establish whether these thresholds predict reduction difficulty, residual dysplasia, or long-term outcomes. The current clinical value of these AUC values and cutoffs is therefore limited to hypothesis generation and preoperative imaging awareness, pending validation in prospective outcome-based studies.

The management and outcomes of inverted LACC during treatment remain subjects of considerable debate. Some scholars oppose the excision of inverted LACC [27], arguing that the labrum is continuous with the lateral acetabular cartilage and lacks a clearly defined boundary. The acetabular cartilage contains secondary ossification centers that contribute to acetabular growth in older children. Accidental resection of this cartilage may lead to the failure of ossification center formation at the acetabular rim during adolescence, resulting in acetabular dysplasia [28,29]. Therefore, they recommend performing a radial incision rather than excision on the labrum when it obstructs reduction. In contrast, other researchers emphasize that an inverted labrum not only impedes hip reduction and development but may also lead to joint instability and long-term functional impairment [20,30], advocating for proactive intervention. However, our study found that in some patients with preoperative inverted LACC, the smooth, arc-shaped morphology of the bony acetabulum has already been altered. In such cases, labral excision may not improve the congruence between the bony acetabulum and the femoral head. As illustrated in Figure 1, this patient developed posterior AOO. Although the femoral head was reduced back into the acetabulum after open reduction, the presence of AOO resulted in persistent femoral head anteversion, indicating that isolated labral incision alone was insufficient to resolve the underlying incongruence. Resection of the inverted acetabular labrum is clinically significant only when the bony acetabular morphology remains unchanged. Thus, we emphasize the importance of preoperative evaluation of the bony acetabular morphology before determining the appropriate management strategy for the inverted labrum.

We found that posterior acetabular involvement was the most common pattern, including isolated posterior and combined anterior–posterior lesions, accounting for 74.1% of AOO-positive hips. While we did not perform quantitative morphological measurements (e.g. acetabular version angle) to confirm biomechanical consequences, the topographic predominance of posterior ossification prompts several hypotheses that are clinically intriguing but remain speculative. We hypothesize that the abnormal ossification in the posterior acetabulum may be associated with excessive anteversion of the femoral head during reduction. Previous studies have shown that some DDH patients exhibit a prominent posterior acetabular wall, which is associated with osteoarthritis [31,32]. We speculate that the abnormal ossification forming in the posterior acetabulum may be linked to this prominent acetabular posterior wall. Meanwhile, the abnormal ossification in the posterior acetabulum could theoretically alter the biomechanical environment of the hip joint. It is hypothesized that this might contribute to a more retroverted acetabular orientation and anterior displacement of the femoral head, potentially triggering mechanical impingement during flexion and abduction. This speculative mechanism might ultimately accelerate cartilage wear and joint dysfunction. Therefore, further evidence-based research is needed to clarify the correlation between the abnormal ossification of the acetabulum in DDH and osteoarthritis.

Radiation exposure is inherent to CT imaging in this pediatric cohort. All examinations were clinically indicated and performed using the pediatric dose-optimized protocols in effect at the time of each examination. Nevertheless, the potential risks of radiation should be weighed against the diagnostic benefits in future applications of this imaging approach.

This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective cross-sectional design precludes any causal or temporal inference. In addition, the two LACC groups were imbalanced in sample size and age distribution. Although we employed multivariable adjustment and stratified analyses to minimize confounding, residual confounding from this baseline imbalance cannot be entirely excluded. Several subgroup odds-ratio estimates had wide confidence intervals, indicating limited precision; therefore, the corresponding effect sizes should be regarded as exploratory. Second, the absence of a healthy control group limits our ability to distinguish pathological ossification from normal developmental variation. Third, although we adjusted for AI and Tönnis grade, residual confounding from unmeasured severity parameters cannot be excluded. Fourth, the CT-based definition of AOO lacks histopathological validation; the term ‘osteophyte-like’ remains descriptive. Fifth, we did not evaluate treatment-related outcomes (e.g. closed reduction failure, need for open reduction, acetabular remodeling, AVN risk, or long-term prognosis), and the lack of longitudinal follow-up precludes prognostic conclusions.

In conclusion, age was the most consistent independent correlate of AOO across the entire cohort. The role of LACC morphology was age-dependent: inverted LACC was strongly associated with ossification exclusively in children >2 years with a posterior predilection. From a clinical standpoint, these findings suggest that preoperative imaging assessment of bony acetabular morphology – particularly in older children (>2 years) with inverted LACC – may help identify AOO and inform surgical planning. Future multicenter prospective studies with standardized protocols are needed to validate these findings, and further investigations incorporating histological validation and longitudinal follow-up are required to establish the prognostic significance of AOO in pediatric DDH management. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating, requiring prospective validation.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: A representative case of unilateral DDH with acetabular osteophyte-like ossification (AOO). a) Preoperative coronal CT shows AOO (arrow) in the right acetabulum. b) Preoperative sagittal CT demonstrates that the AOO is located in the posterior aspect of the right acetabulum(arrow). c) Coronal CT 8 months after open reduction surgery reveals AOO (arrow) in the right acetabulum as well. d) Postoperative sagittal CT shows AOO in the posterior acetabulum(arrow), with increased density and an irregular border of the femoral head. AOO alters the smooth, curved morphology of the acetabulum and results in femoral head anteversion, affecting the congruence between the acetabulum and the femoral head, leading to poor prognosis.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: MRI morphological classification of the labrum-acetabular cartilage complex (LACC) in DDH (arrow). a) Everted LACC. b) Inverted LACC. c) Partly inverted LACC.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Definition of acetabular osteophyte-like ossification (AOO): On serial coronal CT Multi-Planar Reconstruction (MPR) images of the bilateral hip, a circle is outlined to fit the bony acetabulum, using the triradiate cartilage as the landmark. The presence of acetabular bone protruding into this circle is defined as AOO (arrow).

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Representative imaging findings showing the relationship between acetabular osteophyte-like ossification (AOO) and acetabular cartilage. a) Coronal CT image shows bilateral AOO (arrows). b) Corresponding coronal T1-weighted MRI image shows that the bilateral AOO (arrows) were surrounded by relatively thick acetabular cartilage . This imaging correspondence suggests that these lesions may be related to abnormal ossification or developmental irregularity of the acetabular cartilage, rather than representing independent osteophytic proliferation.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: a) The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of age and osteophyte-like ossification in the inverted group. b) The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of age and the abnormal ossification in the everted group.
